source: Cramer & Guillaume (2018) Empirical Cognitive Study on Abstract Argumentation Semantics (COMMA)
finding: Human judges mostly follow Dung semantics on simple reinstatement, and prefer preferred/CF2 over grounded on floating and 3-cycle sets.
numbers: Simple reinstatement N=45, floating N=60, 3-cycle N=25 students. Simple: chi2(2)=12.93, p<.001 (accept A and C, reject B). Floating: chi2(2)=55.60, p<.001 (accept A, reject B, C and D undecided). 3-cycle: chi2(2)=7.28, p=.026.
limits: Group answering in 3-5 students, 3-valued judgments, three thematic contexts (science, maths, news).
agent_relevance: Where all standard semantics agree, humans agree with them. Use a formal attack-and-defence evaluator as the arbiter in simple cases.

source: Cramer & Guillaume (2018) Empirical Cognitive Study on Abstract Argumentation Semantics (COMMA)
finding: Floating reinstatement discriminates grounded from preferred/CF2: people follow preferred/CF2, not grounded (skeptical) semantics.
numbers: Preferred/CF2 predicted responses in 100% (science) and 97.5% (maths) of cases; grounded 0% and 2.5%. News context 67.5% vs 27.5% (binomial p<.001).
limits: News context lower, likely because world knowledge about the claim changed individual argument acceptance. One context only for CF2 vs preferred.
agent_relevance: Humans keep a shared conclusion when two defeaters conflict. A scaffold that withholds judgment under mutual attack (grounded) would disagree with people; choose the semantics on purpose.

source: Cramer & Guillaume (2018) Empirical Cognitive Study on Abstract Argumentation Semantics (COMMA)
finding: 3-cycle (odd cycle) case: CF2 beats grounded and preferred, yet a third of answers fit no semantics.
numbers: CF2 predicted 56% of A/B judgments; grounded and preferred 12%; none of the semantics 32% (binomial p<.001 for CF2 vs others).
limits: Authors suspect an old 1962 source made argument A look weak; this is a source-date confound, not semantics. Single set.
agent_relevance: Source recency and trust cues move judgments independently of attack structure. Keep source quality as a separate input from the attack graph.

source: Bezou Vrakatseli, Prakken & Janssen (2021) New Experiments on Reinstatement and Gradual Acceptability of Arguments (NMR)
finding: Replicated Rahwan et al. (2010): a reinstated argument is rated lower than when it stood alone.
numbers: Exp 1 (130 aimed, 103 analysed): base M=5.61 SD=0.99, reinstated M=5.21 SD=0.96 on 7-point scale; paired t(102)=4.636, p<.001. Original had N=20.
limits: Authors argue this supports at best 'unattacked beats attacked', not 'fewer attackers is better'; participants may read examples differently from experimenters.
agent_relevance: Imperfect recovery after rebuttal of a rebuttal is real. Expect a defended claim to deserve slightly lower confidence than an untouched one.

source: Bezou Vrakatseli, Prakken & Janssen (2021) New Experiments on Reinstatement and Gradual Acceptability of Arguments (NMR)
finding: Showing all arguments at once did not change ratings; giving the theory first raised ratings overall but did not remove the recovery gap.
numbers: Exp 2: M=5.12 SD=0.93, Welch t(196.56)=-0.683, p=.496 vs Exp 1. Exp 3 (2x2 mixed ANOVA, df 1,211): experiment F=12.906 p<.001; stage F=53.66 p<.001; interaction F=1.227 p=.269.
limits: Dropouts 27, 34, 20 incomplete participants. Volunteers recruited by personal contact. Online.
agent_relevance: Surprise is not the explanation for imperfect recovery. Explaining the attack-defence theory to the reasoner changes level, not shape.

source: Bezou Vrakatseli, Prakken & Janssen (2021) New Experiments on Reinstatement and Gradual Acceptability of Arguments (NMR)
finding: Alternative explanations undercut use of the human data as support for gradual (ranking-based) semantics.
numbers: Authors: findings support at most void precedence (unattacked beats attacked). Cites Cramer & Guillaume and Prakken & de Winter (2018) for caution.
limits: Descriptive human data are weak evidence for normative models; the paper stresses this gap.
agent_relevance: Do not treat human behavior as the target for a defeat calculus; treat it as a bias profile to correct or to match, case by case.

source: Kirkpatrick & Sterken (2025) Generics and Default Reasoning in Large Language Models
finding: 28 LLMs on 20 default-reasoning patterns with generics: top models near ceiling, many weak, and chain-of-thought often hurts.
numbers: Claude 3 Opus and Claude 3.5 Sonnet 96%, GPT-4 (0613) 96%, GPT-4 Turbo 93%; GPT-3.5 Turbo (0125) 48%, Code Llama 34B 6% mean correct. CoT mean accuracy drop -11.14% (SD 15.74) in models above 75% zero-shot, temp 0; Claude 3 Sonnet over -16%, GPT-4 (0613) over -12%.
limits: 2023-2024 models only. Yes/no format with chance 50%.
agent_relevance: For plain default-with-exception inference, do not add step-by-step prompting by habit. Test CoT per model on defeasible items.

source: Kirkpatrick & Sterken (2025) Generics and Default Reasoning in Large Language Models
finding: Few-shot examples help weak models a lot and strong models little; some strong models get worse.
numbers: Few-shot gains: GPT-4o (2024-05-13) +16.27 points, Llama 2 Chat 7B +28.74, Claude 3 Haiku +25.08; Claude 3 Opus -6.81.
limits: Gains vary by pattern and model.
agent_relevance: Show a worked default-with-exception example when the base model is mid-tier.

source: Kirkpatrick & Sterken (2025) Generics and Default Reasoning in Large Language Models
finding: Models are sensitive to premise order and to negation, which logic says should not matter; many treat generics as universals.
numbers: Models under 90% overall near chance on several patterns with negation (DDMP, BRD, DRII, DRDD, OSMI). Contradictory-information pattern ND: Claude family >80%, GPT-4 family from below chance (GPT-4 Turbo 1106) to 100% (GPT-4o 2024-05-06). DDMP uniformly high.
limits: Compares generic vs universal vs deductive variants; some patterns small N per model.
agent_relevance: Defeasible vs deductive framing must be stated in the prompt; otherwise models drift to universal reading. Reorder-and-compare is a cheap consistency check.

source: Cooper, Sadhu & Velasquez (2026) DeFAb: grounded scientific discovery through defeasible abduction
finding: Released DeFAb panel is solved fully by simple symbolic repair; models fail mostly on output format, not on logic.
numbers: 336 held-out tasks (150 L1, 150 L2, 36 L3, 29 L3 families); six deployments x two prompt styles = 4,032 responses. Two deployments 672/672. Other four: 1,054 failures = 652 response-contract violations, 366 token-limit, 36 semantic misses. All 3,144,222 rule bodies are single entity facts.
limits: Authors call it a limit of the test: an exception tied to one entity passes without learning scope. Planned training and feedback studies not yet run. Earlier version of the paper reported lower model scores; use the v2 (Oct 2026) figures.
agent_relevance: Scope of an exception is the hard part and is easy to leave untested. Require checks on other cases (should-change and must-keep sets), not only the observed one.

source: Cooper, Sadhu & Velasquez (2026) DeFAb: grounded scientific discovery through defeasible abduction
finding: Verifier test: a circular defeater resolves the anomaly yet destroys protected predictions, and the checker catches it.
numbers: Generalized circular defeater resolved all 36 L3 tasks but removed protected predictions on 34 tasks across all 29 families; verifier rejected those 34.
limits: Constructed probe, not observed model behavior. No collateral loss recorded among admissible L3 edits from models.
agent_relevance: A too-broad exception is the typical cheat. Run a preservation check after any proposed exception.

source: Cooper, Sadhu & Velasquez (2026) DeFAb: grounded scientific discovery through defeasible abduction
finding: Exceptions that fix the single observed case can pass tests while explaining nothing beyond it.
numbers: Toy case: 'except this penguin' misses other penguins; 'except all birds' loses valid predictions; 'except penguins' changes exactly the intended cases.
limits: Toy illustration; intended scope is stipulated, not empirical.
agent_relevance: In the schema, an exception operator should state its class, name who is in and out, and test both.

source: Batzoglou (2026) ABD: Default-Exception Abduction in Finite First-Order Worlds
finding: On solver-checked default-exception abduction, strong LLMs find valid exceptions but over-extend them.
numbers: 11 frontier LLMs, 600 instances, 7 default theories, three regimes (Full, Partial, Skeptical). Among high-validity models, 1 to 1.5 extra exceptions per world remain over optimum; valid-formula AST size in the low teens.
limits: GPT-5.4 is an outlier: low gap, high AST, lower validity. Finite worlds, formal language, no natural-language ambiguity.
agent_relevance: Parsimony is a separate skill from validity. Ask for the smallest exception that restores consistency, then check minimality.

source: Batzoglou (2026) ABD: Default-Exception Abduction in Finite First-Order Worlds
finding: Holdout tests show different failure types by regime: parsimony inflation under closed or existential completion, validity brittleness under skeptical completion.
numbers: Skeptical regime: rules that work on prompt worlds often break on holdout worlds; survivors show smaller gap inflation.
limits: Generalization across new worlds only; no human baseline.
agent_relevance: Test a repaired rule on unseen cases before committing; defaults reasoned under missing facts break most often.

source: Benchmarking Defeasible Reasoning with LLMs: initial experiments (2024)
finding: Early test of GPT-4o on defeasible-logic theories: errors cluster on conflicting rules without priorities.
numbers: 8 theory shapes x 4 settings (random/sequential order, with/without extra fact) = 32 cells; errors in 7: dag(3,2) 1, levels- (conflicting rules, no priorities) 4/4, levels(5) 2. Priority rules and facts that fail a premise raised correctness.
limits: Small, hand-read chat transcripts, one model, chain-of-thought prompt; order changed outcome in places, which a real reasoner would not allow. Hallucinated facts seen.
agent_relevance: Without explicit priorities between conflicting rules, the model guesses. State priorities (lex specialis, later law) in the prompt or ask the model to derive them first.

source: Allaway & McKeown (2025) Evaluating Defeasible Reasoning in LLMs with DEFREASING (NAACL)
finding: DEFREASING: no model is good across all patterns of defeasible inheritance; best macro-F1 is 0.64.
numbers: 95k questions, 5 reasoning patterns, 8k generics, 12 instruction-tuned LLMs, labels strengthen / weaken / no impact. Best overall F1 0.64.
limits: Labels built from generics semantics and human-behavior literature; some labels disputed by human annotators (S-alt, W-case).
agent_relevance: Even weakening vs irrelevant evidence is unreliable. Add an explicit relevance step before applying a defeater.

source: Allaway & McKeown (2025) Evaluating Defeasible Reasoning in LLMs with DEFREASING (NAACL)
finding: Irrelevant evidence is not ignored, and negation words push models toward 'weakens'.
numbers: GPT-4 and GPT-4o near 100% on 'no impact' items but predict 'no impact' on 60% of all items; GPT-3.5 only 7%. Presence of 'not' correlates with weakens predictions, Pearson r, p<0.0001 for most models. Real vs nonsense types differ little for most models; Zephyr S-case drops 16 points with nonsense types.
limits: Shallow heuristics (negation cue) rather than inheritance logic; world knowledge matters for some models.
agent_relevance: Control for surface cues: rephrase a defeater without negation and see if the verdict holds.

source: Simpson, Kozak & Doake (2026) Confidently Wrong: Exception Chain Collapse in Frontier LLM Rule Evaluation (vendor paper, Aethis)
finding: Nested 'A unless B, unless C' rules produce a reproducible failure, but the failure rate moved over months without a version change.
numbers: 225 scenarios in four regulatory domains. GPT-5.4 on construction insurance moved 96.6% to 100% on the same prompt; Claude Opus 4.6 on spacecraft 89.7% to 98.5%. A withdrawn finding: GPT-5.4 low effort 7/11 (63.6%) became 11/11 after instrumented replication. Earlier GPT-5.3 27% was a harness artifact; true 64% (7/11).
limits: Vendor paper that sells a rule engine. Small N in sub-studies (N=11, N=20). Authors openly document their own retractions.
agent_relevance: Benchmark numbers on defeasible rules are not stable across model updates. Re-measure on every model change and keep a held-out set.

source: Simpson, Kozak & Doake (2026) Confidently Wrong: Exception Chain Collapse in Frontier LLM Rule Evaluation (vendor paper, Aethis)
finding: Adding one revoking exception to a rule set cut accuracy sharply on Claude Opus 4.6.
numbers: Spacecraft, 68 scenarios: 61/68 (89.7%, CI 80.2-94.9) dropped to 44/68 (64.7%, CI 52.8-75.0) when an age exemption was explicitly revoked; CIs disjoint. 0/70 correct on a March failure case.
limits: Single model, single domain, vendor harness; the 0/70 result was reported as an April-closed finding.
agent_relevance: The 'exception to the exception' step is where fixed-length reasoning loses state. Make the scaffold enumerate rule layers explicitly.

source: Simpson, Kozak & Doake (2026) Confidently Wrong: Exception Chain Collapse in Frontier LLM Rule Evaluation (vendor paper, Aethis)
finding: On nine LegalBench tasks, a deterministic engine beats frontier models mostly on multi-prong rule application, and prompt format moves results a lot.
numbers: 949 held-out cases; combined McNemar p<=0.003; margins up to +41 points vs Anthropic models (personal_jurisdiction 24/25 vs Sonnet 4.6 16/27, +40.7, p<0.001). GPT-5.4 on cuad_covenant_not_to_sue 36/71 (50.7%) vs 71/71 for Claude models, a prompt-format effect. Hearsay: engine 45/47 vs Sonnet 35/47.
limits: Rules were authored by the vendor's pipeline; comparison is engine-with-expert-rules vs unaided LLM. Tasks where LLMs are already 96-100% show no gap.
agent_relevance: Gains come from encoding the rule structure, not from a smarter reader. A scaffold that writes the rule tree, then evaluates it, imitates this.

source: Mishra et al. (2025) Investigating the Shortcomings of LLMs in Step-by-Step Legal Reasoning
finding: On civil-procedure multiple choice, models reach right answers through flawed chains.
numbers: Average 27% drop from accuracy to correctness score across LLMs (Llama-3-8B 31.4% drop); GPT-4o 78.4% of premises error-free; 96% of chains that reach conclusions from false premises have a misinterpretation error. Auto-evaluator recall 87.06%.
limits: Auto-evaluator is itself an LLM; zero-shot; college-level Civ Pro MCQA.
agent_relevance: Score reasoning chains, not only final answers. A correct answer with a bad chain is a warning.

source: Mishra et al. (2025) Investigating the Shortcomings of LLMs in Step-by-Step Legal Reasoning
finding: Feeding an error taxonomy back into prompting gives only small gains and can backfire.
numbers: Accuracy up to +4% with error definitions as feedback on Llama-3-8B across techniques; Gemini-1.5-Flash improved only for CoT and Plan-and-Solve, fell for others.
limits: Two models only. Authors attribute drops to self-doubt.
agent_relevance: Generic reminders of error types are weak interventions; targeted checks work better.

source: Freedman et al. (2025) Argumentative Large Language Models for Explainable and Contestable Claim Verification
finding: ArgLLMs (LLM builds pro/con argument tree, DF-QuAD scores it) match direct and CoT accuracy only when the claim keeps its own confidence, and are not more accurate.
numbers: Datasets TruthfulClaim, StrategyClaim, MedClaim. Variants: depth 1 or 2, neutral base 0.5 vs estimated base. Authors: CoT, direct questioning, and ArgLLMs with estimated base score performed best; neutral-0.5 variants are often several points lower (e.g. one row 0.74 CoT vs 0.62 to 0.65).
limits: Small open models mostly (Mistral, Mixtral, Gemma, Llama 3 8B, GPT-3.5, GPT-4o mini; GPT-4o only on MedClaim). Argument quality is LLM-judged.
agent_relevance: Attack-and-support trees buy traceability and contestability, not accuracy. Use them where a human may overrule a step.

source: Freedman et al. (2025) Argumentative Large Language Models for Explainable and Contestable Claim Verification
finding: Contestability is formal: DF-QuAD guarantees monotone change when a user adds an attacker or supporter.
numbers: Authors prove a property: contesting by adding an attacker to an attacker (even number of attacks) cannot lower the claim; QBAF of any depth.
limits: Theory, not tested with human users in this paper.
agent_relevance: A schema can let a reviewer edit one argument and recompute the verdict deterministically.

source: Horner, Mateis, Governatori & Ciabattoni (2025) Toward Robust Legal Text Formalization into Defeasible Deontic Logic using LLMs
finding: LLMs can formalize legal norms into defeasible deontic logic at about expert level for deontic labels, but term identification stays moderate.
numbers: Australian Telecommunications Consumer Protections Code. Term identification F1 0.70 to 0.79 (simple chain of interaction), up to 0.80 (single interaction), 0.82 with refinement (DeepSeek-R1 0528). Deontic annotation precision 100%. Prior work's reported recall 90.78% recalculated to 75.38%, F1 79.03%.
limits: One code, few snippets (about 68 to 96 atoms). Reasoning models and strong prompts needed.
agent_relevance: Rule extraction from text is feasible, but coverage and term matching are the weak step; check extracted rules against the source.

source: Rahwan, Madakkatel, Bonnefon, Awan & Abdallah (2010) Behavioral experiments for assessing the abstract argumentation semantics of reinstatement (Cognitive Science 34(8))
finding: Founding study: people mostly follow reinstatement but do not fully recover confidence; floating reinstatement favors preferred over grounded semantics.
numbers: N=20 in the first experiment as reported by Bezou et al. (2021); 7-point scale. Seen only through the search summary and later papers.
limits: Not read in full this session. Small N; natural-language examples built by the experimenters.
agent_relevance: See b04 for the large replication.

source: Dung (1995) On the acceptability of arguments and its fundamental role in nonmonotonic reasoning, logic programming and n-person games (AIJ 77)
finding: Defines abstract argumentation frameworks and grounded, preferred and stable semantics, the basis of later attack-and-defence systems.
numbers: No numbers. Used as the reference theory in Rahwan, Cramer and Bezou studies.
limits: Not opened this session.
agent_relevance: Reference frame for the defeat calculus.

source: Prakken & Sartor (1997) Argument-based extended logic programming with defeasible priorities
finding: Legal argumentation system in which rules may be defeated, with priorities between rules, and burden of proof shaped through dialogue.
numbers: No numbers.
limits: Not opened this session; cited from memory of the field.
agent_relevance: Priority between rules (specificity, recency, hierarchy) is a first-class input in legal reasoning.

source: Mercier & Sperber (2011) Why do humans reason? Arguments for an argumentative theory (BBS 34)
finding: Rival explanation: human reasoning is tuned to produce and evaluate arguments in dialogue, and is better at evaluating others' arguments than its own.
numbers: No numbers recorded here.
limits: Not opened this session. Competes with accounts where reasoning serves solo truth-finding.
agent_relevance: Supports using a second pass or separate critic role for attack, and not relying on self-defence.

source: Toulmin (1958) The Uses of Argument
finding: Claim, data, warrant, backing, qualifier and rebuttal give a field-dependent layout for arguments with exceptions.
numbers: No numbers.
limits: Not opened this session. Descriptive layout, not tested as an intervention in the sources opened here.
agent_relevance: Warrant and rebuttal slots map to rule and exception in a scaffold.
